description: A dynamic duo powerhouse team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge! Combining full-stack development, end-to-end execution, and secure IT infrastructure. Core: Python, Django, Flask, SQL, JS. Skilled in AI tools, data extraction, and high-performance digital solutions. Ready to build something out of this world! ✨
summary: NASA tracks active fires with two sensors, MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), whose counts cannot be compared directly: in our region VIIRS counts 7 to 8.6 times more detections in the same weeks. PyroHistorian converts the MODIS record to the VIIRS scale with an honest uncertainty range, shows it as a burning-activity calendar for a user-selected area, and helps the user decide which faint VIIRS signals deserve action, using MODIS only as an independent check. It runs entirely in the browser.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Satellites have tracked active fires for over two decades, but the record is split between MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012). VIIRS is far more sensitive, so the switch creates a false jump in 2012, and its faint signals make it hard to decide which ones deserve action.

WHAT WE BUILT

1. Harmonization. Detections are counted per grid cell and week. MODIS counts are converted to the VIIRS scale with a monthly ratio estimated from the years both sensors operated, with a low-to-high range instead of a single value. Every cell-week carries a quality code: measured, converted or missing. We tested the conversion by leaving one year out: the real value fell inside the range in 86% of cases, which is about what a min-to-max range should give.

2. Triage. For the years with both sensors, a signal is one grid cell in one week. When VIIRS counts one detection, MODIS also sees that cell 14% of the time; with more than ten detections, 89%. The user picks a threshold and sees its price. At 5 detections the list is 29% shorter, the share of the list also seen by MODIS rises from 65% to 81%, and 90% of confirmed signals are kept; 24% of removed signals were seen by MODIS. A richer score (neighbours, continuity) did not beat strength alone (AUC 0.869 vs 0.875), so we kept the simple rule.

3. Alarm history. Alarm states use a seasonal baseline and hysteresis, ideas borrowed from industrial alarm management. Alarms are historical and the tool never sends commands.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline reads NASA FIRMS files and writes three small JSON files; a browser app (map, triage, calendar, alarm list, validation) computes everything for the selected area. No server and no AI model run at run time.

LIMITS

There is no ground truth: "seen by MODIS" is indirect evidence, and "not confirmed" does not mean "false". We tested one region (10 x 10 degrees in northern Australia) and have not tested the tool with fire managers or operators. There is no validation before 2012. The tool lowers priority and never deletes a signal.

NEXT STEPS

Check against burned-area data or incident records, use fire radiative power and detection time, and prepare for the end of MODIS (the triage rule needs VIIRS only).
dataRefs: NASA Earthdata & FIRMS (MODIS / VIIRS Active Fire Data)
